question.text: Is driving above the posted limit in a highway work zone lawful?

answer.text: Driving faster than the posted speed limit inside a highway work zone is unlawful.

teaching.text: Driving above the posted limit inside a highway work zone is unlawful. Remember: work zone limits are law.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving faster than the posted speed limit inside a highway work zone is unlawful.

question.text: Where does a highway work zone begin and end?

answer.text: A highway work zone runs from the first sign marking where the zone begins to the last sign marking where it ends.

teaching.text: A work zone stretches from the first sign marking its start to the last sign marking its end. Remember: first sign to last sign.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A highway work zone runs from the first sign marking where the zone begins to the last sign marking where it ends.

question.text: When does an extra speeding penalty apply in a work zone?

answer.text: If a sign at the start of a work zone lists a speeding penalty, that penalty is added on top of any other penalty for the speeding conviction.

teaching.text: A speeding penalty listed on the starting sign is added on top of any other speeding penalty. Remember: posted penalty adds on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a sign at the start of a work zone lists a speeding penalty, that penalty is added on top of any other penalty for the speeding conviction.

question.text: How do the work zone boundaries relate to the extra penalty?

answer.text: A work zone begins at the first work zone sign and ends at the last one, and an extra speeding penalty applies only when a sign at the start lists it.

teaching.text: The signs set the zone's limits, and the extra penalty applies only when the start sign lists it. Remember: zone by signs, penalty if posted.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A work zone begins at the first work zone sign and ends at the last one, and an extra speeding penalty applies only when a sign at the start lists it.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: zone by signs, penalty if posted

question.text: What are orange signs with black lettering used for?

answer.text: Orange signs with black lettering are used only to identify work zones, both on the approach and inside the zone.

teaching.text: Orange signs with black lettering are used only for work zones, on the approach and inside. Remember: orange means work zone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Orange signs with black lettering are used only to identify work zones, both on the approach and inside the zone.

question.text: What does a Flagger sign tell you?

answer.text: A Flagger sign means a worker in an orange vest ahead is directing traffic with a STOP and SLOW paddle, so stay alert and be ready to stop.

teaching.text: A Flagger sign means a worker ahead is directing traffic with a STOP and SLOW paddle, so be ready to stop. Remember: flagger ahead, be ready.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A Flagger sign means a worker in an orange vest ahead is directing traffic with a STOP and SLOW paddle, so stay alert and be ready to stop.

question.text: When should you act on a black-on-orange advance sign?

answer.text: Black-on-orange advance signs may tell you to act, such as moving to another lane, and they give that message early enough that you should not wait until the last moment.

teaching.text: Advance black-on-orange signs give early instructions, so act on them without waiting. Remember: act early, not late.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Black-on-orange advance signs may tell you to act, such as moving to another lane, and they give that message early enough that you should not wait until the last moment.

question.text: What is a leading cause of rear-end collisions in work zones?

answer.text: In work zones, going slower than the traffic around you is a leading cause of rear-end collisions, because confined lanes may leave no escape route.

teaching.text: In work zones, going slower than surrounding traffic is a leading cause of rear-end collisions. Remember: too slow causes rear-ends.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In work zones, going slower than the traffic around you is a leading cause of rear-end collisions, because confined lanes may leave no escape route.

question.text: Which devices guide drivers through a work zone?

answer.text: Barricades, cones, drums and flaggers are the traffic control devices used to guide drivers safely through a work zone.

teaching.text: Barricades, cones, drums and flaggers guide drivers through a work zone. Remember: cones, drums, barricades, flaggers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Barricades, cones, drums and flaggers are the traffic control devices used to guide drivers safely through a work zone.

question.text: When does North Carolina law require headlights?

answer.text: North Carolina law requires headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever you cannot see more than four hundred feet ahead.

teaching.text: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and whenever you cannot see four hundred feet ahead. Remember: sunset to sunrise, or low visibility.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: North Carolina law requires headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever you cannot see more than four hundred feet ahead.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: sunset to sunrise, or low visibility

question.text: What are the two triggers that require headlights?

answer.text: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and also whenever visibility drops to four hundred feet or less, even in daytime.

teaching.text: The visibility trigger applies even in daytime, alongside the sunset to sunrise rule. Remember: dark or under four hundred.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and also whenever visibility drops to four hundred feet or less, even in daytime.

question.text: When must you turn on headlights because of your wipers?

answer.text: North Carolina requires every driver to turn on headlights whenever the windshield wipers are in use because of bad weather.

teaching.text: Whenever the wipers are on because of bad weather, headlights must be on too. Remember: wipers on, lights on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: North Carolina requires every driver to turn on headlights whenever the windshield wipers are in use because of bad weather.

question.text: When should you use low beams and high beams at night?

answer.text: At night use low beams in the city, and on the open road use high beams except when approaching or following another vehicle.

teaching.text: At night, use low beams in the city and high beams on the open road unless near other vehicles. Remember: low in town, high open.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night use low beams in the city, and on the open road use high beams except when approaching or following another vehicle.

question.text: Why is driving at night riskier?

answer.text: Night driving is riskier because visibility is lower, more impaired and tired drivers are out, and oncoming headlights can blind you.

teaching.text: Night brings lower visibility, more impaired and tired drivers, and blinding oncoming lights. Remember: less light, more risk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Night driving is riskier because visibility is lower, more impaired and tired drivers are out, and oncoming headlights can blind you.

question.text: What should you do if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on?

answer.text: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, blink your high beams once as a reminder; if they still do not dim, stay on low beam.

teaching.text: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, blink yours once, then stay on low beam. Remember: blink once, stay low.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, blink your high beams once as a reminder; if they still do not dim, stay on low beam.

question.text: If an oncoming driver will not dim, should you switch to high beams?

answer.text: Flash your high beams once to remind an oncoming driver to dim, but if they do not, keep your own lights on low rather than switching to high beams.

teaching.text: One reminder blink, then keep your own lights on low. Remember: remind once, stay on low.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Flash your high beams once to remind an oncoming driver to dim, but if they do not, keep your own lights on low rather than switching to high beams.

question.text: How should you avoid oncoming headlight glare at night?

answer.text: To avoid headlight glare at night, slow down and look slightly toward the right edge of the road instead of into oncoming lights.

teaching.text: Slow down and look toward the right edge of the road to avoid oncoming glare. Remember: eyes to the right edge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid headlight glare at night, slow down and look slightly toward the right edge of the road instead of into oncoming lights.

question.text: How fast is too fast at night?

answer.text: Never drive so fast at night that you could not stop within the stretch of road you can actually see.

teaching.text: At night, drive slowly enough to stop within the road you can actually see. Remember: stop within your sight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive so fast at night that you could not stop within the stretch of road you can actually see.

question.text: What lights should you use when parked beside a highway at night?

answer.text: When parked on or beside a highway at night, turn on the emergency flashers and switch off the headlights so they do not blind oncoming drivers.

teaching.text: Parked beside a highway at night, use the flashers and switch off the headlights. Remember: flashers on, headlights off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When parked on or beside a highway at night, turn on the emergency flashers and switch off the headlights so they do not blind oncoming drivers.

question.text: What should you do about sun glare?

answer.text: For sun glare, lower the visor and wear sunglasses; if that is not enough, pull off to the roadside until you can drive safely.

teaching.text: For sun glare, use the visor and sunglasses, or pull off until you can drive safely. Remember: visor, sunglasses, or pull off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For sun glare, lower the visor and wear sunglasses; if that is not enough, pull off to the roadside until you can drive safely.

question.text: What must you use in rain, and how should your speed change?

answer.text: In rain you must use your headlights and wipers, and you should drive more slowly than normal.

teaching.text: Rain means headlights, wipers and a slower speed than normal. Remember: rain means lights, wipers, slower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In rain you must use your headlights and wipers, and you should drive more slowly than normal.

question.text: How much longer can stopping take on slippery pavement, and what following gap should you allow?

answer.text: Stopping on slippery pavement can take from two to ten times as far as on dry pavement, so allow at least double the usual following distance.

teaching.text: Slippery pavement can stretch stopping distance two to ten times, so at least double your following gap. Remember: double the gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stopping on slippery pavement can take from two to ten times as far as on dry pavement, so allow at least double the usual following distance.

question.text: How does the wet-road stopping multiplier compare with the following-distance rule?

answer.text: Wet pavement can stretch stopping distance from two to ten times, which is why the following gap should be at least doubled.

teaching.text: Stopping can stretch two to ten times, while the following gap should at least double. Remember: stopping grows, gap doubles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wet pavement can stretch stopping distance from two to ten times, which is why the following gap should be at least doubled.

question.text: When are roads slickest during rain, and why?

answer.text: Roads are slickest in the first ten to fifteen minutes of rain, when water mixes with oil, dirt, dust and rubber on the surface.

teaching.text: Roads are slickest in the first ten to fifteen minutes of rain, as water mixes with oil, dirt, dust and rubber. Remember: first minutes are slickest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Roads are slickest in the first ten to fifteen minutes of rain, when water mixes with oil, dirt, dust and rubber on the surface.

question.text: How much slower should you drive on wet pavement?

answer.text: On wet pavement drive at least five to ten miles per hour slower than you would on dry pavement.

teaching.text: On wet pavement, drive at least five to ten miles per hour slower than on dry pavement. Remember: wet road, five to ten slower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On wet pavement drive at least five to ten miles per hour slower than you would on dry pavement.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: wet road, five to ten slower

question.text: When should you avoid cruise control?

answer.text: Never use cruise control during or after rain, because the time spent switching it off in a hydroplane could cost you control.

teaching.text: Never use cruise control during or after rain, since switching it off in a hydroplane takes time. Remember: no cruise in rain.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never use cruise control during or after rain, because the time spent switching it off in a hydroplane could cost you control.

question.text: Is cruise control fine once the rain has stopped?

answer.text: Cruise control stays off not only while it rains but also after the rain, since releasing it during a hydroplane costs time you may not have.

teaching.text: Cruise control stays off after the rain stops, not only while it falls. Remember: off during and after.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cruise control stays off not only while it rains but also after the rain, since releasing it during a hydroplane costs time you may not have.

question.text: What is hydroplaning, and how early can it start?

answer.text: Hydroplaning happens when a thin layer of water lifts the tires off the road, and it can begin at speeds as low as thirty miles per hour in water just over one eighth inch deep.

teaching.text: Hydroplaning lifts the tires on a thin layer of water and can start as low as thirty miles per hour. Remember: water lifts the tires.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning happens when a thin layer of water lifts the tires off the road, and it can begin at speeds as low as thirty miles per hour in water just over one eighth inch deep.

question.text: What should you do if your car hydroplanes?

answer.text: If you hydroplane, lift your foot off the gas, do not brake, keep the wheel straight and let the car slow until the tires grip again.

teaching.text: If you hydroplane, ease off the gas, do not brake, keep the wheel straight and let the car slow. Remember: ease off, no brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you hydroplane, lift your foot off the gas, do not brake, keep the wheel straight and let the car slow until the tires grip again.

question.text: What speed can start hydroplaning, and what is the response?

answer.text: Hydroplaning can start at about thirty miles per hour in water just over one eighth inch deep, and the response is to ease off the gas without braking.

teaching.text: Hydroplaning can begin around thirty miles per hour, and the answer is easing off without braking. Remember: thirty can hydroplane, ease off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning can start at about thirty miles per hour in water just over one eighth inch deep, and the response is to ease off the gas without braking.

question.text: How do tires affect hydroplaning risk?

answer.text: Deep, open tire tread helps prevent hydroplaning, while worn or under-inflated tires raise the risk; for skid handling, tire pressure on the high side of the maker's range is better.

teaching.text: Deep, open tread helps prevent hydroplaning, while worn or under-inflated tires raise the risk. Remember: deep tread fights hydroplaning.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Deep, open tire tread helps prevent hydroplaning, while worn or under-inflated tires raise the risk; for skid handling, tire pressure on the high side of the maker's range is better.

question.text: What are signs of standing water on the road?

answer.text: Signs of standing water include reflections on the surface, dimples from raindrops, a slushing tire sound and a loose feel in the steering.

teaching.text: Reflections, raindrop dimples, a slushing sound and loose steering signal standing water. Remember: reflections, dimples, slushing, loose.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signs of standing water include reflections on the surface, dimples from raindrops, a slushing tire sound and a loose feel in the steering.

question.text: How long after rain can puddles cause hydroplaning?

answer.text: Puddles left by rain can cause hydroplaning for hours or even days after the rain stops.

teaching.text: Rain puddles can cause hydroplaning for hours or even days afterward. Remember: puddles linger for days.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Puddles left by rain can cause hydroplaning for hours or even days after the rain stops.

question.text: What share of North Carolina tropical-weather deaths since nineteen seventy came from inland flooding?

answer.text: Since nineteen seventy, inland flooding has caused eighty-five percent of tropical-weather deaths in North Carolina, and half of those involved people driving onto roads known to be flooded.

teaching.text: Since nineteen seventy, inland flooding has caused eighty-five percent of tropical-weather deaths in the state. Remember: floods cause most storm deaths.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Since nineteen seventy, inland flooding has caused eighty-five percent of tropical-weather deaths in North Carolina, and half of those involved people driving onto roads known to be flooded.

question.text: Should you drive through standing water on a road?

answer.text: Never drive through standing water on a road, since it may be deeper than it looks and part of the road may be washed out.

teaching.text: Never drive through standing water, which may be deeper than it looks or hide a washed-out road. Remember: turn around, never through.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive through standing water on a road, since it may be deeper than it looks and part of the road may be washed out.

question.text: How much fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and how much can float it?

answer.text: About six inches of fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and about twelve inches can float it or roll it over.

teaching.text: About six inches of fast water can sweep a car away, and about twelve inches can float or roll it. Remember: six sweeps, twelve floats.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: About six inches of fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and about twelve inches can float it or roll it over.

question.text: How do the sweeping depth and the floating depth differ?

answer.text: About six inches of fast water can sweep a car off the road, while about twelve inches can float or overturn it.

teaching.text: Six inches of fast water can sweep a car off the road, and twelve inches can float it. Remember: six inches sweeps away.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: About six inches of fast water can sweep a car off the road, while about twelve inches can float or overturn it.

question.text: What should you do if fog is so thick you can barely see?

answer.text: If fog is so thick you can barely see, pull well off the road, stop, secure the car, turn on the flashers, exit on the passenger side and stay away from the road.

teaching.text: In fog too thick to see, pull well off, stop, use the flashers, exit on the passenger side and stay away. Remember: pull far off, exit right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If fog is so thick you can barely see, pull well off the road, stop, secure the car, turn on the flashers, exit on the passenger side and stay away from the road.

question.text: If you must drive in fog, which lights and habits help?

answer.text: If you must drive in fog, use low beams, slow down, watch for the taillights ahead and keep an eye on vehicles behind you.

teaching.text: Driving in fog means low beams, a slower speed, and watching taillights ahead and vehicles behind. Remember: low beams, slow, watch taillights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you must drive in fog, use low beams, slow down, watch for the taillights ahead and keep an eye on vehicles behind you.

question.text: How does handling thick fog differ from driving in lighter fog?

answer.text: In thick fog you pull far off and exit on the passenger side, while in drivable fog you use low beams and watch for the taillights ahead.

teaching.text: Thick fog means pulling off and getting out on the passenger side, while drivable fog means low beams and care. Remember: thick, stop; light, low beams.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In thick fog you pull far off and exit on the passenger side, while in drivable fog you use low beams and watch for the taillights ahead.

question.text: Which road spots are often the first to freeze?

answer.text: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots are often the first places to freeze as temperatures fall.

teaching.text: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots are often first to freeze. Remember: bridges freeze first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots are often the first places to freeze as temperatures fall.

question.text: How much should you slow down on packed snow and on ice?

answer.text: In a snowstorm, slow down and use wipers and low beams; cut speed by more than half on packed snow and slow to a crawl on ice.

teaching.text: In a snowstorm, use wipers and low beams, cut speed by more than half on packed snow, and crawl on ice. Remember: half speed, crawl on ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a snowstorm, slow down and use wipers and low beams; cut speed by more than half on packed snow and slow to a crawl on ice.

question.text: How should you start moving on snow or ice?

answer.text: On snow or ice, speed up gently, test your steering and braking feel, and in a manual car start in second gear or higher with a slow clutch release.

teaching.text: On snow or ice, accelerate gently, test steering and braking, and start a manual car in second gear or higher. Remember: gentle starts, test grip.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On snow or ice, speed up gently, test your steering and braking feel, and in a manual car start in second gear or higher with a slow clutch release.

question.text: How much stopping distance should you allow on snow or ice, and how should you stop?

answer.text: Allow at least three times the normal stopping distance on snow or ice, and when stopping keep off the brake so the engine slows the car.

teaching.text: Allow at least three times the normal stopping distance on snow or ice, and let the engine slow the car. Remember: triple the stopping room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Allow at least three times the normal stopping distance on snow or ice, and when stopping keep off the brake so the engine slows the car.

question.text: On snow or ice, should you stop with the brake pedal or the engine?

answer.text: On snow or ice allow at least three times the normal stopping distance, and to stop you lift off the brake and let the engine do the slowing.

teaching.text: Three times the stopping room, and the engine does the slowing instead of the brake pedal. Remember: let the engine slow you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On snow or ice allow at least three times the normal stopping distance, and to stop you lift off the brake and let the engine do the slowing.

question.text: Can chains and snow tires make quick moves safe on ice?

answer.text: Chains and snow tires can still slide on ice and packed snow, so you cannot start, stop or steer quickly in those conditions.

teaching.text: Chains and snow tires can still slide, so no quick starts, stops or turns on ice or packed snow. Remember: chains still slide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Chains and snow tires can still slide on ice and packed snow, so you cannot start, stop or steer quickly in those conditions.

question.text: How can you reduce wildlife collisions?

answer.text: Wildlife collisions can be reduced by slowing down and scanning road edges, especially at dawn, dusk and into the night.

teaching.text: Slow down and scan the road edges, especially at dawn, dusk and into the night. Remember: slow down, scan edges.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wildlife collisions can be reduced by slowing down and scanning road edges, especially at dawn, dusk and into the night.

question.text: Why does a slower speed matter in a deer strike?

answer.text: Slower speed improves survival for both deer and driver: a deer hit at thirty-five miles per hour is far less likely to be fatal than one hit at fifty-five miles per hour or more.

teaching.text: A deer hit at thirty-five miles per hour is far less likely to be fatal than one hit at fifty-five or more. Remember: slower hit, better survival.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slower speed improves survival for both deer and driver: a deer hit at thirty-five miles per hour is far less likely to be fatal than one hit at fifty-five miles per hour or more.

question.text: When are animals most active?

answer.text: Animals are most active at dawn, at dusk and in the first few hours after dark, and spring and fall migrations call for extra caution.

teaching.text: Animals are most active at dawn, dusk and the first hours after dark, and during spring and fall migrations. Remember: dawn, dusk, after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Animals are most active at dawn, at dusk and in the first few hours after dark, and spring and fall migrations call for extra caution.

question.text: When should you use high beams where animals may be?

answer.text: Use high beams only when there is no oncoming traffic and no animal right ahead, since bright lights can freeze some animals in place.

teaching.text: Use high beams only with no oncoming traffic and no animal right ahead. Remember: no oncoming, no animal ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use high beams only when there is no oncoming traffic and no animal right ahead, since bright lights can freeze some animals in place.

question.text: Why avoid high beams when an animal is directly ahead?

answer.text: Use high beams only with no oncoming traffic and no animal directly ahead, because bright beams can freeze some animals in the road.

teaching.text: Bright beams can freeze some animals, so dim them when an animal is directly ahead. Remember: bright lights freeze animals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use high beams only with no oncoming traffic and no animal directly ahead, because bright beams can freeze some animals in the road.

question.text: After you see one deer, what should you expect?

answer.text: Many animals such as deer travel in groups, so after seeing one, expect others to follow close behind.

teaching.text: Deer often travel in groups, so expect more after you see one. Remember: one deer means more.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Many animals such as deer travel in groups, so after seeing one, expect others to follow close behind.

question.text: What should you do when an animal is in the roadway?

answer.text: When an animal is in the roadway, hold your lane and brake firmly to stop if you can; a short honk of the horn is also an option.

teaching.text: For an animal in the road, hold your lane and brake firmly, and a short honk is an option. Remember: hold the lane, brake firmly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When an animal is in the roadway, hold your lane and brake firmly to stop if you can; a short honk of the horn is also an option.
